items.title: 15.3.1 Generation and Transmission of Nerve Impulse

source_refs.note: Topic 15.3.1 with its For Information and Tidbit boxes (PDF 30-32); Figures 15.4 and 15.5 (both printed as 15.5) are replaced by original diagrams.

blocks.text: 1 Before the impulse: resting membrane potential

A resting neuron, not carrying a signal, is polarized: negative inside and positive outside. Its membrane potential, the resting membrane potential (RMP), is about -70 millivolts; the minus sign means the inside is negative relative to the outside. Three factors set it up.

items: Fixed anions: large negatively charged molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids are more abundant inside the cell and cannot diffuse out.

The sodium-potassium pump: K+ is about 30 times more concentrated inside than outside and Na+ about 10 times more concentrated outside. Pumps in the membrane use ATP to move these ions against their gradients, three Na+ out for every two K+ in, so the inside becomes more negative.
K+ leakage: some K+ ions leak out through K+ gates. This exit of K+ and the retention of negatively charged proteins are the major factors for the RMP.

blocks.text: When a neuron becomes active, the membrane potential at one region reverses so that the inside becomes positive relative to the outside. This is the active membrane potential, or action potential, produced by these events.

items: Depolarization: Na+ gates open and Na+ rushes in, cancelling the negative charge inside; the potential goes from -70 mV through zero to +50 mV, on a short region for about one millisecond.
Repolarization: Na+ gates close and K+ gates open; K+ diffuses out and the inside becomes negative again.
Hyperpolarization: because the K+ gates are slow to close, the potential briefly goes a little more negative than the RMP. The neuron cannot fire again during this refractory period.
Return to RMP: the sodium-potassium pump restores the original ion distribution and the membrane returns to -70 mV, ready for the next action potential.

blocks.alt: Top: a strip of neuron membrane with Na+ about ten times higher outside and K+ about thirty times higher inside, large negative fixed anions inside, a sodium-potassium pump moving 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in using ATP, and a K+ leak channel. Bottom: a graph of membrane potential against time: flat at -70 mV, a steep rise to +50 mV (as printed), a fall below -70 mV and a slow return to -70 mV.
blocks.caption: Factors responsible for the RMP, and the generation of an action potential (original diagram after Figures 15.4 and 15.5).
blocks.long_description: At rest the inside of a neuron is about -70 mV: fixed anions stay inside, the pump moves three Na+ out for every two K+ in, and K+ leaks out. During an action potential Na+ gates open and Na+ rushes in (depolarization, up to +50 mV as the book gives it, for about a millisecond); then Na+ gates close and K+ gates open, K+ flows out (repolarization) and briefly overshoots (hyperpolarization, the refractory period) before the pump restores -70 mV.

blocks.text: Action potentials do not really travel along the axon; they are reproduced at neighbouring regions. An action potential in one region acts as a depolarizing stimulus for the next, which produces its own action potential, while the previous region repolarizes back to the RMP.

blocks.alt: Top: a non-myelinated axon with + charges outside and - inside except in one red active region where the charges are reversed; an arrow shows the active region moving on as the region behind repolarizes. Bottom: a myelinated axon with blue myelin segments and red curved arrows jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next. A note gives speeds of 1 to 3 m/s without myelin and up to 120 m/s with it.
blocks.caption: Propagation of an action potential (original diagram after the second Figure 15.5).
blocks.long_description: An action potential does not itself travel: each active region depolarizes the next, which fires its own action potential, while the region behind repolarizes. Its strength stays the same along the axon. In a myelinated axon action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier and jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), up to 50 times faster than in the fastest non-myelinated axons.

blocks.title: A stadium wave
blocks.text: Propagation is like a 'wave' in a stadium: each person stays in place, stands up (depolarizes), raises the hands (action potential) and sits down again (repolarizes), and the wave moves round.
